r1-p14-001: html:The analysis first compared the peak frequency of the normal baseline 0-0 with each weight condition. By the rate of change in peak frequency, Δf = (f<sub>condition</sub> − f<sub>baseline</sub>) / f<sub>baseline</sub> × 100 (%), the 1-1 condition showed a clear drop of −8.9%, while 1-0 was detected not by a frequency change but by changes in RMS, the band-energy features and the Autoencoder reconstruction error. This shows that even a low-cost MEMS sensor can detect changes in dynamic properties due to changes in mass distribution. On a small foam-board model, however, differences in manual excitation, the sensor's fixing and cable movement may affect the natural frequency more than temperature and humidity do, so the temperature/humidity-compensation effect was not concluded from the model experiment alone but cross-checked against the openLAB analysis in 2.7; the result is reflected in the difference in exceedance rates between the uncompensated and temperature/humidity-compensated models.
s1-p01-023:
html:4. Results
In the model-bridge experiment, adding 100 g on the left and right lowered the first peak frequency by 8.9%, confirming detection of mass change, and temperature/humidity compensation improved the F1 score about 4.9-fold, from 0.075 to 0.370, and the false-alarm rate in the humidity segment from 17.5% to 9.1%. On full-scale bridge data from Germany's openLAB, the false-alarm rate also decreased consistently after compensation.
s2-p01-017:
html:1. Project topic
We developed a low-cost first-stage bridge vibration screening system that observes vibration and the environment together with a MEMS accelerometer and a temperature/humidity sensor, compensates for normal variation explained by temperature and humidity, detects only the remaining change as anomaly candidates, and also shows the bands that departed.
s2-p01-020:
html:3. Differences from existing work (solutions)
Existing low-cost MEMS studies do not address environmental compensation, KRISS's fiber-optic (BOCDA) precision measurement requires dedicated infrastructure, and unsupervised studies on public data mostly stop at outputting an anomaly score. This project is distinguished by integrating measurement, environmental compensation, anomaly judgment and band-wise explanation into a single low-cost device.
s2-p01-021:
html:4. Results
In the environment × mass × bolt experiment with 27 conditions (1,380 windows), the compensated model detected all 840 damage windows (recall 100%, F1 0.998), with 4/90 false alarms (4.4%). Over 5 repeated seeds, only the compensated model kept 100% for every seed (uncompensated 96.2–99.3%). The anomaly score grew with the severity of damage (5.8× → 22.6×), and bolt loosening (40–80 Hz) and mass change (amplitude/energy) were distinguished by their contributing features. The reduction in false alarms from compensation was confirmed in the humidity segment of the stage-1 experiment, 17.5% → 9.1%, and was reproduced in the same direction on full-scale openLAB data.
s3-p01-017:
html:1. Project topic
We developed a low-cost first-stage bridge screening system that records vibration and the environment together with a MEMS accelerometer and a temperature/humidity sensor, compensates for normal variation explained by temperature and humidity, alerts only on the remaining change as anomaly candidates, and also shows which vibration characteristic departed.
s3-p01-020:
html:3. Differences from existing work (solutions)
Existing low-cost MEMS studies do not address environmental compensation, fiber-optic (BOCDA) precision measurement requires dedicated infrastructure, and unsupervised studies on public data mostly stop at outputting an anomaly score. This project integrates measurement, environmental compensation, anomaly judgment and explanation of causes into a single low-cost device and validated it directly, from model experiments to real pedestrian overpasses.
s3-p01-021:
html:4. Results
In the 27-condition environment × mass × bolt experiment on the aluminum model, the compensated model detected all 840 damage windows (recall 100%) with false alarms on only 4 of 90 normal windows (4.4%), and its contributions distinguished bolt loosening from mass change. On public openLAB data, once the frequency channel was combined, temperature compensation reduced the autumn false-alarm rate from 26% to 0–3%. On two real overpasses, mode peaks were tracked within 1%; with a 200 kg load the frequency fell by 0.6% and returned after removal, and alarms sounded only in the loaded state, not in the unloaded state.
